text: A single qubit lives in a 2-dimensional vector space. Two qubits don't live in a 4-element list of two separate 2-dimensional spaces — they live in one genuinely 4-dimensional space, and the Kronecker product is the exact operation that builds it.

np dot kron takes every entry of one matrix and multiplies it by the entire second matrix, tiling the results into one larger structure. Two single-qubit states combine into a 4-dimensional two-qubit state, with each of the four basis states landing in its own slot. The same operation builds multi-qubit gates, and which qubit a gate targets depends on where in the Kronecker product it appears. Each additional qubit doubles the dimension, two to the n for n qubits — the source of both quantum computing's power and classical simulation's cost.

Building the four two-qubit basis states is direct: kron of ket-zero and ket-one gives zero, one, zero, zero, that's the state ket-zero-one. kron of ket-one and ket-zero gives zero, zero, one, zero, state ket-one-zero. Which position holds the one is exactly the binary number the two qubits spell out.

CNOT, controlled-NOT, flips the target qubit only when the control qubit is one. Built as kron of P-zero and I, plus kron of P-one and X, and tested on the real state ket-one-zero, it returns zero, zero, zero, one, exactly ket-one-one. The target flipped from zero to one precisely because the control was one — CNOT's entire defining behavior, confirmed numerically rather than just asserted.

Next lesson is the chapter's lab: putting the at-sign operator, transpose, conjugate, np dot linalg dot eig, and np dot kron together, finishing with the single most important sanity check in quantum computing — confirming a matrix is actually unitary.
